name: Gaetano Scirea

early_history_summary: Born to a working-class family in Cernusco sul Naviglio, Scirea began playing football in the streets and was spotted by local coach Gianni Crimella at age 10. He joined Atalanta's youth academy at 14, made his Serie A debut at 19, and transferred to Juventus at 21, where he became a legendary sweeper.
family_context_summary: Born to a Sicilian factory worker father who spent 35 years at Pirelli and a Lombard mother who also worked for 34 years; working-class family with four children in the Milan suburbs.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family background in football; father was a factory worker at Pirelli with a passion for Inter Milan but no professional connection to the sport.

evidence_summary: Scirea grew up in a working-class family in the Milan suburbs with no football connections, but benefited from Italy's robust youth football pipeline. He was spotted by a local coach at 10, joined Atalanta's youth academy at 14, and made his Serie A debut at 19. His transfer to Juventus at 21 placed him in one of Europe's elite clubs, where he formed a legendary defensive partnership with Claudio Gentile and Antonio Cabrini. By 26, he was an established Juventus starter and Italian international.
starting_point: Born to a working-class family in Cernusco sul Naviglio near Milan; father was a Sicilian factory worker at Pirelli for 35 years, mother also worked for 34 years; third of four children.
current_position: Died in a car accident in Poland on September 3, 1989 at age 36; final role: Juventus defender and captain, 78-cap Italian international.

trajectory.event: Made his Serie A debut for Atalanta against Cagliari on September 24, beginning his professional football career.
Transferred to Juventus, where he would spend his entire remaining career and become one of the greatest defenders in football history.

Won the European Cup with Juventus, completing the rare feat of winning all major UEFA club competitions.
Retired from professional football after 14 seasons at Juventus with seven Serie A titles and numerous international trophies.
Died in a fatal car accident in Poland on September 3 while on a scouting trip for Juventus.

name: Justin Rose
milestone_by_age_26: Won his first European Tour title at the Dunhill Championship in Johannesburg on January 20, 2002 at age 21, after famously finishing tied for fourth at the 1998 Open Championship as a 17-year-old amateur.
early_history_summary: Born in Johannesburg, South Africa, Rose moved to England at age 5 and was introduced to golf by his father Ken, a former tennis player turned golfer, who taught him from 11 months old with a plastic club. He left school at 16 to focus on golf full-time, finished T4 at the 1998 Open at 17, turned pro, then endured 21 consecutive missed cuts before breaking through with his first European Tour win at 21.
family_context_summary: Father Ken Rose was a useful tennis player in South Africa who took up golf and taught Justin from toddlerhood; the family was middle-class and could not afford a full-time coach, so Ken studied the swing and taught Justin the fundamentals himself. Ken died of cancer in 2002 at age 57.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father Ken was a golfer who personally coached Justin from age 11 months, teaching him the fundamentals of the swing; this was a direct, sustained domain transfer from parent to child.
primary_early_advantage_tags: father as golf coach, early start at 11 months, North Hants Golf Club at 12, T4 at Open at 17, Walker Cup team
evidence_summary: Rose's father Ken, a South African who swapped tennis for golf, introduced Justin to the sport at 11 months and served as his primary coach throughout his childhood, teaching him the fundamentals when they could not afford a professional coach. Justin joined North Hants Golf Club at 12, made the Walker Cup team as a teenager, and famously finished T4 at the 1998 Open at 17 before turning pro. After missing 21 consecutive cuts, he won his first European Tour event at 21 in Johannesburg, the city of his birth.
starting_point: Born in Johannesburg, South Africa to a middle-class family; father Ken was a former tennis player turned golfer who introduced Justin to golf at 11 months; family moved to Hampshire, England when Justin was 5.
current_position: Active PGA Tour golfer at age 45 with 13 PGA Tour wins; former World No. 1; lost Masters playoff to Rory McIlroy in 2025; resides in England and the US.

trajectory.event: Finished tied for fourth at the Open Championship at Royal Birkdale as an amateur, chipping in on the 72nd hole, and turned professional immediately after.
Won his first European Tour title at the Dunhill Championship in Johannesburg, breaking through after missing 21 consecutive cuts as a rookie professional.
Won the US Open at Merion, his first major championship, becoming the first Englishman to win the US Open since 1970.
Won the Olympic gold medal in golf at the Rio Olympics, the first Olympic golf gold since 1904.
Reached World No. 1 in the Official World Golf Rankings for the first time in his career.
Lost a sudden-death playoff to Rory McIlroy at the Masters, his second Masters playoff defeat, while remaining competitive on the PGA Tour at age 45.

name: Camilla Herrem

family_context_summary: Both parents played handball, and her brother Carl-Åge and sister Cathrine also played, creating a family environment fully immersed in the sport from childhood.

She started at Sola HK, made her Norwegian League debut at 16, and debuted for the Norwegian national team at 19 in 2006. Being born in Norway, the dominant nation in women's handball, gave her access to the world's best training environment and competitive pipeline. By 25, she had won European Championship gold and Olympic gold.
starting_point: Born in Sola, Norway (near Stavanger) to a handball family; both parents played handball, as did her brother Carl-Åge and sister Cathrine, creating a sport-immersed household.
current_position: Retired from the Norwegian national team in December 2024 after 332 caps and 951 goals; continues playing for Sola HK in the Norwegian league and Champions League while undergoing cancer treatment; widely regarded as one of the greatest handball players of all time.

trajectory.event: Made her debut in the Norwegian handball league for Sola HK, beginning her professional career.
Made her debut for the Norwegian national team against Sweden on April 5, beginning a 332-cap international career.
Won her first European Championship gold medal with Norway at the 2008 European Championship in Macedonia.
Won Olympic gold with Norway at the London 2012 Olympics, defeating Montenegro 26-23 in the final.
Won the World Championship gold with Norway, becoming the most successful player in World Championship history with three golds.
Won her second Olympic gold at the Paris 2024 Olympics and her sixth European Championship gold, then retired from the national team with 332 caps and 951 goals.

name: Francois Botha
milestone_by_age_26: Scored a notable professional upset victory over former cruiserweight contender Mike Hunter in Reno, Nevada on November 22, 1992 at age 24, establishing himself on the US boxing scene after an extensive amateur career with approximately 300 fights and South African national colours.
early_history_summary: Born in Witbank, South Africa, Botha started boxing at age 6 at his father's encouragement, had an extensive amateur career with approximately 300 fights and 30-plus titles, won South African colours twice, worked as a fireman, and turned professional in February 1990 at age 21 before moving to the US to pursue boxing full-time.
family_context_summary: Father was an amateur rugby player who encouraged Francois to take up boxing as a hobby outside school; working-class background in Witbank, South Africa; Botha worked as a fireman before turning professional.
parent_family_domain_summary: Father was an amateur rugby player who wanted his son to take up a sport outside the school curriculum of rugby and cricket; he encouraged boxing but was not a boxer himself.
primary_early_advantage_tags: boxing from age 6, 300 amateur fights, South African colours, fireman background, Mike Hunter upset at 24
evidence_summary: Botha grew up in a working-class family in Witbank, South Africa, where his father, an amateur rugby player, encouraged him to box from age 6. He lost his first four amateur fights but persevered to compile approximately 300 amateur bouts and win South African national colours twice. A right arm injury at 16 left him with permanent nerve damage, but he continued boxing and worked as a fireman before turning professional at 21. His notable upset win over Mike Hunter at 24 in the US established him on the international boxing scene.
starting_point: Born in Witbank, South Africa to a working-class family; father was an amateur rugby player who encouraged boxing as a hobby from age 6; worked as a fireman before turning professional boxer.
current_position: Retired from professional boxing in 2014 with a record of 48 wins, 11 losses, and 3 draws; last known residing in Newport Beach, California; also competed in kickboxing and MMA.

Scored a notable upset victory over former cruiserweight contender Mike Hunter in Reno, Nevada, gaining attention in the US boxing scene.
Won the IBF heavyweight title against Axel Schulz in Germany, but was stripped after testing positive for nandrolone and the result was changed to No Contest.
Fought Mike Tyson in Las Vegas, losing by TKO in the fifth round after leading on the scorecards early in the fight.
Challenged Lennox Lewis for the WBC and IBF heavyweight titles, losing by TKO in the second round.
Fought his final professional boxing match, finishing with a career record of 48 wins, 11 losses, and 3 draws.

name: Luca Cordero di Montezemolo
milestone_by_age_26: Appointed sporting director of Scuderia Ferrari in 1974 at age 26, having been personally recruited by Enzo Ferrari the previous year to serve as his assistant at the legendary Formula One team.
early_history_summary: Born into an aristocratic Piedmontese family in Bologna, Montezemolo graduated with a law degree from La Sapienza University in Rome in 1971 and studied international commercial law at Columbia University. He appeared on a radio program discussing Ferrari's fortunes, which caught Enzo Ferrari's attention, leading to a personal recruitment in 1973 and appointment as sporting director of Scuderia Ferrari in 1974.
family_context_summary: Born into an aristocratic Piedmontese family; father Massimo was a marchese whose family served the Royal House of Savoy for generations; grandfather and great-grandfather were Italian Army generals; uncle was a naval admiral; mother was niece of a famed surgeon.
parent_family_domain_summary: No direct family connection to automotive or motorsport industries; the family's domain was military service and aristocratic administration, but their social network provided access to Italy's business elite including the Agnelli family that controlled FIAT and Ferrari.
primary_early_advantage_tags: aristocratic family, Royal House of Savoy, La Sapienza law degree, Columbia University, Enzo Ferrari mentor, Agnelli family connection, FIAT/Ferrari network
evidence_summary: Montezemolo was born into a prominent aristocratic Piedmontese family with generations of military service to the Royal House of Savoy, providing elite social networks and financial security. He graduated from La Sapienza in Rome and studied at Columbia, then was personally recruited by Enzo Ferrari in 1973 after appearing on a radio program. His childhood friend Cristiano Rattazzi was the son of Susanna Agnelli, connecting him to the FIAT dynasty. By 26, he was sporting director of Scuderia Ferrari, one of the most prestigious positions in motorsport.
starting_point: Born into an aristocratic Piedmontese family in Bologna; father was a marchese whose family served the Royal House of Savoy for generations; grandfather and great-grandfather were Italian Army generals; elite social standing with connections to Italy's business establishment.
current_position: Former chairman of Ferrari (1991-2014) and FIAT; net worth estimated at approximately $350 million; involved in various business ventures including NTV high-speed trains and family investment company.

trajectory.event: Graduated with a law degree from La Sapienza University in Rome, then moved to New York to study international commercial law at Columbia University.
Was personally recruited by Enzo Ferrari to join Scuderia Ferrari as his assistant, beginning a lifelong association with the marque.
Appointed sporting director of Scuderia Ferrari, overseeing the Formula One racing team at one of motorsport's most storied organizations.
Led Ferrari to the Formula One World Championship with Niki Lauda, re-establishing Ferrari as a dominant force in F1.
Appointed president of Ferrari by FIAT chairman Gianni Agnelli, tasked with reviving the struggling company.
Began presiding over Ferrari's most successful era, winning eight Formula One Constructor's World Championships between 1999 and 2008 with Michael Schumacher.
Resigned as Ferrari chairman after being squeezed out by FIAT's Sergio Marchionne, ending a 23-year tenure at the helm.

name: Dragutin Šurbek
milestone_by_age_26: Won the European Championship Men's Singles title in Lyon in 1968 at age 22 as a complete outsider, beating Hungarian defender Janos Börzei in a physically exhausting final, after joining the Yugoslav national team at 20.
early_history_summary: Born in Zagreb, Yugoslavia, Šurbek's father was killed in a car accident when he was 7. He started playing table tennis at age 10 at the STK Poštar club, was largely self-taught, won his first Cadet Boys' title at 14, joined GSTK Vjesnik in 1965, and made the Yugoslav national team at 20 before his breakthrough European Championship win at 22.
family_context_summary: Father was killed in a car accident when Dragutin was 7 years old, creating a difficult childhood; he largely taught himself to play table tennis without parental guidance in the sport.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family background in table tennis documented; father died when Dragutin was young, and he was largely self-taught with no sustained coaching in his early years.
primary_early_advantage_tags: self-taught, father killed at 7, STK Poštar at 10, first title at 14, Yugoslav national team at 20, European champion at 22, supreme fitness
evidence_summary: Šurbek grew up in Zagreb with a difficult childhood after his father was killed in a car accident when he was 7. He started playing table tennis at 10 at the STK Poštar club and was largely self-taught, developing supreme fitness and a fearsome forehand. He won his first title at 14, joined GSTK Vjesnik in 1965, and made the Yugoslav national team at 20. His breakthrough came at 22 when he won the European Championship singles title in Lyon as a complete outsider, beating the Hungarian defender Janos Börzei in a final so physically demanding that Börzei had to be carried from the hall.
starting_point: Born in Zagreb, Yugoslavia; father was killed in a car accident when Dragutin was 7, creating a difficult childhood with no documented family support for table tennis.
current_position: Died on July 15, 2018 in Zagreb at age 71; final status: one of the greatest table tennis players in history with 36 medals at World and European Championships and 503 appearances for Yugoslavia.

trajectory.event: Won his first table tennis title in a local Cadet Boys' Singles competition in Zagreb, receiving a cup full of table tennis balls as the prize.
Joined the Yugoslav national table tennis team, beginning a 37-year international career with 503 appearances for Yugoslavia.
Won the European Championship Men's Singles title in Lyon as a complete outsider, beating Hungarian defender Janos Börzei in a physically exhausting final.
Won the World Championship Men's Doubles gold medal in Pyongyang with Antun Stipančić, his first world title.
Won his second World Championship Men's Doubles gold medal in Tokyo with Zoran Kalinić.
Competed at the Barcelona Olympic Games as the oldest athlete, representing newly independent Croatia.
Died on July 15 in Zagreb, leaving a legacy as one of the greatest table tennis players in history with 36 major championship medals.

name: Mark Edmondson
milestone_by_age_26: Won the 1976 Australian Open singles title at age 21 as an unseeded player ranked No. 212 in the world, defeating Ken Rosewall in the semifinals and John Newcombe in the final, remaining the lowest-ranked Grand Slam winner in ATP history.
early_history_summary: Born in Gosford, NSW, Edmondson started playing tennis at age 3 and was coached from age 10 by Charlie Hollis, the legendary coach who had trained Rod Laver. He was the No. 3 junior in Australia but received no financial support from Tennis Australia, working construction and cleaning windows to fund his career before his improbable 1976 Australian Open victory.
family_context_summary: Father had a construction company in Gosford and died of brain cancer during Edmondson's early career; Edmondson worked at his father's construction company and cleaned windows at a hospital to fund his tennis career, receiving no financial support from Tennis Australia.
parent_family_domain_summary: No family background in tennis; father ran a construction company and Edmondson worked there to save money for his tennis travels; the family was working-class to lower-middle-class.
primary_early_advantage_tags: Charlie Hollis coaching from 10, Rod Laver's coach, No. 3 junior in Australia, worked odd jobs, Australian Open win at 21, lowest-ranked Grand Slam winner
evidence_summary: Edmondson grew up in Gosford, NSW, where he was fortunate that Charlie Hollis, the coach who trained Rod Laver, moved to his hometown when Edmondson was 10. Hollis coached him for six years, making Edmondson a disciple of the same methods that produced one of tennis's all-time greats. Despite being the No. 3 junior in Australia, Edmondson received no financial support and worked construction and as a hospital janitor to fund his career. His father's death from brain cancer added financial hardship. At 21, ranked No. 212, he won the Australian Open in one of tennis's greatest upsets.
starting_point: Born in Gosford, NSW, Australia; father ran a construction company and died of brain cancer during Edmondson's early career; working-class to lower-middle-class family with no tennis background.
current_position: Retired tennis player; builds and resurfaces tennis courts in Sydney; plays golf off a 10 handicap; last Australian man to win the Australian Open singles title.

trajectory.event: Qualified for the Australian Open and Wimbledon, earning his first ATP ranking points and reaching a ranking of No. 212.
Won the Australian Open as an unseeded player ranked No. 212, defeating Ken Rosewall and John Newcombe, remaining the lowest-ranked Grand Slam winner ever.
Won the first of four Australian Open doubles titles, establishing himself as a top doubles player.
Reached the Wimbledon singles semifinals and achieved a career-high singles ranking of No. 15.
Won the Davis Cup with Australia and continued his successful doubles career.
Won the French Open doubles title, his fifth Grand Slam doubles title.
Inducted into the Australian Tennis Hall of Fame in January 2007.

name: Pierre Agostini
milestone_by_age_26: No material milestone by age 26 found; he was still a doctoral student at Aix-Marseille University at 26, completing his PhD in 1968 at age 27. His pioneering attosecond physics work and Nobel Prize came decades later.
